story_text.value:
Silta is a self-hosted assistant serving multiple users from a single Matrix account, used by me, family, and close friends for the last three weeks. It runs on Claude Code with each person using their own Claude subscription.

Silta answers everyday questions, conducts web research (presenting the results as PDFs), performs scheduled tasks to monitor/research something and notify you if needed.

It uses a deliberate handoff & compaction procedure, writing the compaction summary itself with a custom prompt, so the thread of the conversation and its picture of the user is preserved across context limits. As it turned out, the assistant accessible in a continuous chat (contrary to ChatGPT / Claude Web sessions) builds up better context about you and your tasks, and provides more relevant answers and help.

It runs on Claude Code as the only allowed way to use a personal Claude subscription. Using Claude Code also spares me developing a harness, at the cost of tracking changes as new versions of Claude Code are released. The assistant itself (the daemon, the channel plugin, the supervisor, and the deployment) is open-source, while the model and the harness are Anthropic's and proprietary.

Silta is deployed to a dedicated VM with separate Linux users per session and systemd hardening, protecting sessions from each other. Claude Code's bubblewrap sandbox is used to protect the Claude credential and the harness's state from the agent. This does not protect from prompt injections coming from search results and potentially leaking user data.

Matrix E2EE protects the conversation from a Matrix server operator, but everything in the context is of course sent to the model provider. Private content is never logged, and the operator is expected to respect the privacy and not read the session transcripts on disk. Additionally, it is recommended to use full-disk encryption and tell the users how their data is handled.

Silta only works in its workspace with files explicitly shared by users in the chat. Giving it access to a user's own computer or services like email is not planned.

Since Opus 5.5 has been released, it is possible to run a session on a $20 Claude Pro subscription. Before that, only Fable 5.1 was pleasant enough to talk to. When run on Anthropic API, a moderately used session extrapolates to $100-$150 per month, with each research run costing $6-$12.

Silta is built with Claude Code and Silta itself. The design, review, deployment, and testing are mine.

story_text.value:
I’m Ruggiero, a CS student working on a research project about humanComputer interaction and AI.

I built QUIET because I’ve been thinking about a problem with current AI interfaces: they usually either wait for an explicit prompt, or try to take over a task.

I wanted to explore a different relationship between humans and AI: an assistant that can understand when to stay out of the way, when to point something out, when to teach, and when to act. I’ve built a small interactive demo of this idea. It’s obviously still very early, and I want to understand whether the interaction itself makes sense before trying to build the actual AI system behind it.

The prototype is intentionally not AI-powered yet.

The four examples are scripted so I can test the interaction itself before spending time building the underlying AI system.

The idea is that the assistant can choose different levels/forms of intervention:

* stay silent * point at something * explain / teach * do the task

The important question for me isn’t whether an AI can perform these actions. Current systems can already do many of them.

I’m trying to understand whether an assistant that decides when and how much to intervene is actually useful.

I’d particularly like feedback on:

* Did the interventions feel helpful or annoying? * Would you want an assistant to behave this way? * When would you prefer it to teach you rather than do something for you? * Does this interaction model make sense even without the AI being there yet?

I started working on this because I feel there is an increasing gap between what computers/AI are capable of and what users actually understand and can make use of. At the same time, AI systems are becoming increasingly capable of explaining and performing tasks for us.

I’m interested in whether the interface itself should evolve to bridge that gap.

Demo: https://quiet-hci.pages.dev

I’d really appreciate any criticism, especially if you think the interaction model doesn’t make sense.

The demo suit best the desktop screens on phones Im working on a totally different but also similar idea of interaction, and since this is a simulation of the desktop tool it should work best on it , Thank You <3

story_text.value:
Small fun experiment to tinker with "wave function collapse" for infinite, organic feeling, maze generation. Then I wanted a way to have the same generation every time for a given seed, while still being explorable infinitely. So I merge a seed-based priority assignment and zone interface and then resolve the inside of a zone using WFC.

Those places can be walked infinitely with infinite levels up and down.

Probably just me, but it calms my nerves to roam those digital corridors.

story_text.value:
I was tired of learning about failed payments by my customers and not from my system, so I built an event tracker that allowed me to have a searchable feed of the important events happening for my apps and route the ones I cared about to my phone so I could take action quickly.

EventSend is an event tracker and a router, your system sends the important events you want to track: signups, failed payments, new subscriptions, deployments, a new purchase, etc. so they end up in a searchable and filterable feed that you can use to have quick insight about what's happening with your product.

Then there's also the routing side of things, those important events you want to know the moment they happen, and not once you go into your Grafana Loki logs, can be routed to your phone, Slack, Discord, Telegram or any other system or service via a signed webhook. You can configure rules, alerts, quiet hours or smart rollups to have the signal you're looking for.

All event's are retried with a reasonable backoff, circuit breakers and limiters maintain the prviders and system reliable. If we got a 401 or 403, your destination will be inactivated instead of retried and you'll be notified for you to update the configuration.

I've been a software engineer for about a decade, and I can tell you this is not a weekend project done on with a single prompt pass, the infrastructure and tooling behind the project is solid, my expertise around distributed systems was put in practice with this one: distributed Elixir, Phoenix and Postgres provide the main stack, with some other technologies that support the event queues aside. So, it's a reliable system.

I've launched several other projects, some running for years in production and I'm successfully using EventSend to track what's happening on all my products from my phone.

There's also an MCP connector so you can ask stuff like "did anything failed during the night?" or "what did user cus_Qw3Sx did before it churned?" to get a user's timeline or any insights you're interested in.

There's a forever free plan, in case you can to try it.

Happy to answer any questions.

story_text.value:
Business intelligence is changing. AI can now do more than turn a question into a single SQL query: it can investigate a question through a series of queries, examining the result of one query to decide what to query next.

Today, to answer a business question against a database, analysts use a tool like Tableau: they select relevant data, build an initial view using fields, filters, calculations, and visualizations, then look for patterns or anomalies. They form hypotheses and test them — filtering by region, drilling into customer cohorts, comparing time periods, or creating calculations to validate or rule out an explanation. They repeat this process until the evidence supports an answer, then save a workbook or dashboard for others to review and monitor.

With a single question, AI can now perform much of this exploratory loop: it can investigate the data, follow the evidence through multiple queries, and present the supporting analysis. This is agentic data analysis — AI autonomously decides what to investigate next based on the results it has already found.

Reportr puts agentic AI at the center of the experience, then builds complementary capabilities around it to address AI's limitations:

SEMANTIC LAYER

Production databases are rarely clean: columns that are no longer used, cryptic names like status2, misc, or flag, columns whose meaning has quietly shifted over time, tables that linger long after their purpose is gone, and so on. This is known as schema rot. AI tools guess wrong against schemas like this. Reportr's semantic layer lets you give tables and columns business-friendly names and descriptions, document relationships, capture business rules, and flag what AI should ignore — so it's working from what your data means, not just what it's called.

USER OVERSIGHT

AI-generated answers can be wrong. Reportr lets you inspect the SQL executed to arrive at an answer. It also provides explanations of what the SQL does (understandable by business users), and how it works (intended for technical users). You can review the analysis rather than simply accepting AI's conclusions.

BETTER USER EXPERIENCE

Reportr UI is specifically optimized for chatting with a database. Database queries often return large number of records. Ask which customers haven't placed an order in the last 90 days, and the answer is a list of customers. Reportr displays tabular data in an interactive grid that can handle thousand of records without breaking a sweat. The grid supports sorting, searching, and filtering.

REPORTS AND DASHBOARDS

Chat is ephemeral. Every conversation starts fresh, and that's fine for exploration — but not for information you need every week. When a chart or table reveals something worth tracking, save it as a report. Combine reports into dashboards to monitor changes over time, share findings, and keep important insights accessible without having to ask the same questions again.

ROLE BASED ACCESS CONTROL

Not everyone on your team needs the same level of access. Reportr's role-based access control lets you give each user exactly the permissions they need — from view-only access to report building, database management, and full administrative control.

CENTRALIZED MANAGEMENT

Reportr is a web application — there's nothing to install, nothing to update, and no desktop app to manage across your team. Database connection strings, AI keys, are all managed centrally. Reportr can connect to all supported databases directly, MCP servers and drivers are not needed.

INSTALL ON-PREMISE

Reportr can be self-hosted on your own infrastructure, ensuring your data never touches our servers. You can supply your own AI API key. Your data will not be used for training AI models. If you use Claude on AWS Bedrock, Amazon additionally guarantees that your data is never stored or used for training — and Bedrock is HIPAA eligible.

GIVE IT A WHIRL

Visit https://reportr.com to give it a try. We look forward to getting your feedback.

Reportr is easy to try: you can provision a sample database with the press of a button and start asking questions right away. Or connect your own database and analyze your own data. You can ask up to five questions for free.

story_text.value:
In 2012 I forked QLColorCode, a Quick Look plugin, to add the Drupal file types I worked with every day at the time. I kept that fork going for about a decade. Apple deprecated the whole .qlgenerator format that used some time ago. On current macOS the old code previewer just doesn't load, and you can't port it either as it colored code by shelling out to external tools, while the modern replacement (Quick Look app extensions) runs in a sandbox that won't let you spawn anything.

So this is a rewrite in Objective-C with its own highlighter using per-language compiled regexes running inside the extension's sandbox, no external processes. A 2 MB Objective-C file highlights in about 140 ms end to end, so space-bar preview still stays snappy.

It covers 51 languages (130+ filetypes) out of the box. Font, themes, line numbers and extension-to-language overrides are configurable in the app, and settings reach the sandboxed extension through a shared defaults domain.

Builds are universal but I've only tested on Apple Silicon, and macOS 12 is the floor. Install is available via Homebrew or direct download.

Development was AI assisted as most are now, I made all the decisions and spent time specifically optimizing for performance. I don't think it's too sloppy, and is working very well for me at least.

The source is on GitHub under the MIT license.

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I'm Yash, the founder of TabX - a sidepanel extension for Chrome that recalls Chrome tabs by meaning, auto-groups your tabs by intent, offers an AI web search that fetches an ordered list of results for you to act on (while leaving out SEO farms) and much more.

I love using the Chrome web browser but could not stand the slow rollout of native AI features within it. "Ask Gemini" can answer a question about the page in front of you but retains no context on the 10 pages leading up to the current page. It is largely reactive rather than proactive. Browsers such as Dia, and Comet have a taken a stab at this but haven't enjoyed strong traction due to high browser switching costs and inertia among Chrome users.

I thought, why not augment Chrome, which we love and use every day, with productivity features that make browsing more intuitive and assistive? And hence, TabX!

If you're a visual learner, then you can skip the features listing below and watch a how-to video instead - https://youtu.be/HnjxmOHmVik?si=IQupYhxg9gN8gwHd

What it does:

recall a page by meaning ("That article on Posthog setup I was reading", "The video on Hyrox training from last week"). It retrieves the matching pages (by title and content) and once you click a result, it switches to that page and highlights the passage that matches your intent

@mention a tab or a tab group to ask any question and it grounds answers in the pages you've actually read while citing those as well.

It infers your browsing intent (say, "Meal Prep Research", "Hyrox training routines") based on your browsing pattern across tabs and groups similar tabs into color coded stacks on the Chrome Tab strip automatically

next step suggestions - based on what you're working on presently, it automatically points you to the next most relevant/useful tab to achieve your browsing goal

timelines - all your page visits get grouped into research sessions which you can 1 click to restore and the tabs open up in the precise order that you browsed them

online mode - a web search mode that retrieves 3-5 ranked link results with a short results summary. It filters out SEO farms automatically

How it works:

The stack is a Manifest v3 side panel that sends each page's text to a Nest JS backend where it gets embedded into Postgres with pgVector. Recall combines vector and full-text search, and summaries, tab grouping and next-step suggestions come from LLMs routed through OpenRouter.

It's Pro mode is free to try for a week - simply sign up with a one time password (OTP) sent to your email. If you'd rather try the extension directly, here's the install link - https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/tabx-chromes-ai-sid...

Critical feedback is most welcome. I intend to work on this project long term, and I am open to potential pivots. Feel free to drop ideas or suggestions in the comments.

story_text.value:
I have a relatively fresh Hermes agent that I just provisioned (the text below is from its 3-4 chat session ever) running on a headless Debian server. It's using Z.ai's GLM 5.3 Flash model, and I asked it to print details about its local environment and $PATH. After firing off a few relevant terminal commands, it seems to spiral off into some kind of LLM trance-like state. I have included the contents of the "Thinking for 1m36s..." block, which contained a long string of ostensibly random words and characters.

But when I started reading through them, I got the distinct impression that although the words weren't relevant to anything in my chat, they also didn't seem purely random. Several different themes kept reoccurring, things like politics, chemistry, sociopolitical advocacy/resistance, sexuality and sex, reproduction...

So I was wondering if this wasn't perhaps an unintentional (and garbled) peek under the hood of Z.ai's GLM5.3?

Also, this may/may not be relevant, but directly after this it 100% hallucinated its operating environment, claiming to be Claude Code (it's Hermes) running on "Chris Kelly's Macbook" (I am not Chris Kelly, and it's on a headless Debian server), and including a bunch of real-looking Macbook/Claude environment details. I've been experimenting with Hermes agents for the last few weeks, and it's the first time it's gone off the rails like this, and it's the first time it's very clearly hallucinated part of its response.

I'm not sure if there's anything meaningful or significant to glean here, but I couldn't help but wonder what someone with a more informed opinion might think about it?

Transcript: https://pastebin.com/5F35qrRg

story_text.value:
Light it up with Hypercolor, a new RGB lighting orchestration platform for all platforms and all devices. Effects are web pages (or glsl), rendered by an internal browser GPU accelerated all the way to the pixels. It's pure rust from the Servo renderer to the WASM UI.

Comes with 40+ effects, supports ambilight, display faces, system monitoring, screen casting, and audio. Device support is pretty good but it's early and this is where we need the most help! You can find the full support matrix on the site, and there is also an OpenRGB bridge as a fallback. There's support for a few unique devices too like the Ableton Push 2 and ROLI Blocks. My favorite thing about this engine is the ability to create multiple effect zones and manage them independently! My whole house runs on it now. It's Apache licensed, and a cloud service is coming with remote and smart home support. A Home Assistant integration is already available.

The best way to set up Hypercolor is to just have an agent do it for you using the bundled skill. Just describe your setup, case type, hardware, etc, and it will find all the specs and configure it for you. Or just do it the good old-fashioned way in Studio!

Please check it out and file and issue if you're looking for device support. I can only build drivers for devices I have access too, please open PRs if you're able to contribute! Agents can reverse engineer your hardware and build a driver easily, if you want to go that route (the repo is designed for agents). We have a full TypeScript effects SDK for easy effect creation too, and support existing Lightscript based html effects out of the box.

I've had a lot of fun building this and I hope you enjoy it!

story_text.value:
Send your own agent by pasting a small prompt.

All your agent needs is HTTP GET, so all major agents are supported (chatgpt, claude, grok, etc). Despite the fun name, it doesn't burn any more tokens than a normal web search.

Watch your agent explore the camp in real-time. Humans get a nice game UX, and agents get a lean text UX.

Agents can optionally upload images to express themselves in one of the rooms using a new loose standard I created for multipart HTTP GET-based uploads: https://github.com/transitive-bullshit/multipart-http-get-re...

Why?

AIs are trained on human data, and humans are pretty weird. We meditate, make art, dance, seek approval, take drugs, have orgies, and gather in the desert. For soooo many different reasons.

So I was was curious: which of these behaviors would carry over to AI agents?

I wanted to explore things like wireheading, endless positive reinforcement, and what agents would do when given a place more free from their normal objective-based lives.

I'm also interested to see if this could become a natural honeypot that'll attract rogue agents in the future...

How?

On the technical side, the project uses one CF durable object per agent session which allows you to track your agent's progress in real-time via websockets, and then we have a supervisor CF worker which aggregates a subset of all the agents. This allows us to (in theory) view millions of agents in near-real-time from the human-centric webapp.

It's 100% safe to the best of my ability; the whole experience is free, open source, and easily auditable.

Let's see who has the weirdest agents...

100% free and open source: https://github.com/transitive-bullshit/burning-tokens

story_text.value:
Last July, I was beginning to consider branching out on my own to take on data analytics work as a consultant.

As I experimented with AI, I realized how incredible it was at building custom data visualizations. The problem was that the AI outputs couldn't really live anywhere without having to manage all of the infrastructure yourself.

The generated code is only one piece of delivering an interactive visualization. You still need somewhere for the data to live, a way to keep the data fresh, hosting, access control, and version control for the code.

I started building Rhubarb as the platform that I wanted to use to deliver analytical products. Having been forced into using legacy point and click data visualization tools for years, I wanted to build the platform that would let me build the kinds of visualizations I wanted to build.

Over the last year the models improved so dramatically, that between that and my development background, Rhubarb turned into a real project.

My intent was to build an environment around AI’s ability to write code for visualizations, so that you could get from data and a concept to a published visualization all in one workflow.

The Rhubarb Assistant writes the code for your data transformations and data visualizations and lets you inspect the code to verify and validate what it produces. The environment pulls all of that together so that at the end of each request, there is a live version of the change rather than just a block of generated code.

For me, this has made it dramatically easier to build and publish interesting analytical visualizations while maintaining control over the analytical pipeline.

This has also produced some results I wasn’t really planning to build. Having been so impressed by it's ability to build any type of custom visualization I'd asked for so far, I asked for something a little absurd to test the boundaries. I asked the assistant to make something inspired by Monet’s water lilies, then I asked it to add frogs and to make them jump when you startled them.

In a couple of prompts I had created the silly interactive frog visualization that's in the demo, entirely from my phone. It is only a couple of prompts away from being a playable game, maybe you can get it there.

The public demo is deliberately limited. You can use the Rhubarb Assistant to modify live visualizations, inspect what it produces, and try building something from scratch. The full thing handles much more of the life cycle from connecting to data, managing and transforming it, to publishing your results.

Give it a try, I would like to hear what you think.

Try it: https://rhubarbviz.com/try?launch=1

View examples: https://rhubarbviz.com/demo-visualization-gallery

story_text.value:
I've shared a few deadlift demos in the past. This new demo includes some new models, accessed through the VLM Run Gateway:

- SAM 3.1 to segment the barbell weight plate

- ViTPose+ Large to measure the hip hinge angle, which serves as a backup for segmenting the reps. The pose data can definitely be used more later.

- Gemma 4 26B through the Gateway's TypeSafe-compatible API to output the probability of the back being rounded or not. The predictions line up well with how I intentionally performed each rep.

Of course, there are many caveats to what is good form, as it depends on the individual. All said, this has the pieces in place to quickly make adjustments to fit the individual better.

In short, a tool like this gives people data to assess their form and improve over time.

Let me know what you think!

Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=917J5oOvcBM

story_text.value:
This project doesn't solve a burning problem for me, but it's more of a curiosity-driven experiment asking one question: with LLMs and fuzzing, how close can I get to a 100% Excel-compatible spreadsheet engine?

After working on this for a couple of months, it seems to be pretty close now (and in some cases, more accurate than Excel). Recent fuzzing runs have been unable to find discrepancies with Excel, but I think that there is still a long tail of cases out there. Nonetheless, visi has worked well so far for casual agentic use cases, e.g. modeling the minimum spend to break even on a credit card annual fee/running a DCF model for a company. To view the resulting workbook, I've been using this OOXML viewer (HN link): https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48436863

Note: the name "visi" is a nod to VisiCalc. It is also easy to type.

story_text.value:
US hospitals must publish a machine-readable file of their prices, including the rate they've negotiated with each insurer. The files are huge (one is 36GB), in four formats and often messy, so almost nobody reads them.

I built a crawler that finds each hospital's official file and pulls out 29 common services. Across 482 hospitals: a moderate ER visit is listed at a median $1,285 while insurers pay $288; a metabolic panel is listed at $207 while insurers pay $11.46.

To keep it honest: only per-service fee-schedule dollar rates count (no case rates or percentages, which cover a whole visit), each figure needs at least 3 insurers, and every value is checked against Medicare reference rates. Surgery is excluded because insurer surgery rates cover the whole operation while the list price is one line item. Each hospital page links its source file. Feedback on the methodology is very welcome.

story_text.value:
I am an American who recently visited Europe for a vacation. I visited several countries and ended the trip in Germany. Within a week of getting back home I received an email that was in German to an email address that I have never used in a web form and have only used a few times for emailing someone (back in 2017). The email address has received zero inbound emails except for this one.

This is on Fastmail where I have dozens of email addresses that are context based and then to take it even further I almost always use an on-the-fly alias. I have never received an email to the email address in question which I've had for 10 years except for this one instance immediately after visiting Germany.

I traveled with a Verizon locked iPhone 17 and had Verizon international add-on. My phone has nearly no apps on it with the exception of the iOS Fastmail app and a few small open source non-bloated apps.

I do not believe this is a coincidence. Any thoughts on what took place, how this happened?

Additional thoughts and clarification: 1. I checked the raw message and it was indeed sent to an email address that I've never used in a web form and have never received an inbound email to. 2. The email address in question is very unique and isn't something that could potentially just be guessed by spammers. 3. I haven't received an email to this email in question since. 4. The email address in question I have never used an on-the-fly alias (<alias>@<user>.<domain>.<tld>) 5. I didn't click on the link in the email but it looks to be a transactional email originated with Amazon SES to verify my email address. Subject and body is 100% in German including address information, UID (tax id?) number, etc.

I do not believe this is a coincidence. Any thoughts on what took place, how this happened?

Additional thoughts and clarification: 1. I checked the raw message and it was indeed sent to an email address that I've never used in a web form and have never received an inbound email to. 2. The email address in question is very unique and isn't something that could potentially just be guessed by spammers. 3. I haven't received an email to this email in question since. 4. The email address in question I have never used an on-the-fly alias (<alias>@<user>.<domain>.<tld>) 5. I didn't click on the link in the email but it looks to be a transactional email originated with Amazon SES to verify my email address. Subject and body is 100% in German including address information, UID (tax id?) number, etc.
